# Applied Materials, Inc. (AMAT) — Munger/Buffett Read

## Circle of Competence
Applied Materials makes the machines that make chips — deposition, etch, ion implant, and inspection/metrology tools sold to a handful of foundries and memory makers. As a business model, this is understandable: sell high-margin capital equipment plus a recurring parts/service annuity into an oligopolistic customer base with high switching costs once a tool is qualified into a process. The underlying physics of each tool is specialist engineering, but the economics — picks-and-shovels for the chip industry, cyclical, concentrated customers — are graspable. Inside the circle, with the caveat that judging *which* process step wins share requires real homework.

## Moat & Durability — Score: 7/10
AMAT is one of three credible suppliers of leading-edge wafer fab equipment (alongside ASML and Lam Research/Tokyo Electron). Once a tool is designed into a customer's process flow, re-qualifying a competitor's alternative is slow, expensive, and risky for the chipmaker — that's real switching-cost moat. Gross margin (49.0%) and operating margin (31.9%) are strong and support the pricing-power read. The Applied Global Services segment (parts, upgrades, service on a large installed base) adds a less-cyclical, higher-margin layer. The moat's weak point isn't competitive — it's structural: wafer-fab-equipment spending is one of the most cyclical capital-goods categories that exists, tied to memory/logic capex cycles that can swing 20%+ in either direction, and a meaningful piece of historical revenue has come from China, which is subject to export-control policy outside the company's control. Real moat; not immune to the cycle or to Washington.

## Management & Capital Allocation
The packet has no direct visibility into insider ownership, management tenure, buyback pace, or dividend policy — a genuine gap, not a judgment. What the ratios imply is favorable on its face: ROE of 39.7% is excellent, and it's achieved with only moderate leverage (debt/equity ~30%, not aggressive) — leverage is not doing the heavy lifting for that return. The more interesting flag is the earnings-vs-cash gap: trailing P/E of 50.8x implies roughly $8.4B of net income, but a 0.71% FCF yield implies only about $3.0B of free cash flow — a large wedge, most plausibly explained by heavy capex for a capacity buildout (which may be growth investment, not a red flag) but that's an inference this packet can't confirm. Before trusting the capital-allocation story implied by strong ROE, I'd want to see the actual capex breakdown (maintenance vs. growth) and buyback/dividend history in the filings.

## Predictability
Semicap equipment is not a boringly consistent business — it is one of the more cyclical corners of industrials/tech, with WFE spending following memory and logic capex booms and busts. The packet's own multiples say as much: a 50.8x trailing P/E against a 31.6x forward P/E implies the market is underwriting roughly 60% forward earnings growth, an unusually steep assumption for a mature capital-goods leader and a sign that current results (or estimates) are anything but steady-state. Momentum adds to the caution: +204.9% over 12 months, +77.8% over 6 months, still +41.6% above the 200-day moving average, but a -8.4% pullback in just the last month — RSI of 52 suggests the extended trend has recently cooled rather than being freshly bid. The `momentum.thesis` field is null, so there's no qualitative color to lean on. Net: this reads as 'too hard, right now' by Munger's easy-decision standard — not because the business is incomprehensible, but because the earnings and price trajectory currently embed more optimism than the historical cyclicality of this industry usually rewards.

## Inversion — How the Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Cyclical air pocket**: WFE spending has historically fallen sharply after capex surges (memory oversupply, logic capex digestion); at 50.8x trailing / 31.6x forward earnings and 46x EV/EBITDA, there is zero room in the price for a normal down-cycle, let alone a sharp one.
2. **China/export-control policy risk**: semicap equipment sales to China have historically been a large slice of industry revenue; further tightening of U.S. export controls is a real, binary, and uncontrollable risk to the revenue base baked into current estimates.
3. **Cash-conversion disappointment**: a 0.71% FCF yield against a 39.7% ROE and rich multiples means today's earnings quality is not obviously translating into distributable cash; if the capex driving that gap doesn't taper the way the market's ~60% forward-earnings-growth assumption requires, the stock has a long way to fall on an earnings miss alone.

## Valuation — Owner Earnings
The packet doesn't give a share price or count directly. Backing into a price with an estimated ~800M shares outstanding against the $428.1B market cap implies a current price near **$530-540/share** — consistent with the 12-month momentum data (a 12-month return of +204.9% off a much lower base). At that share count, trailing net income (market cap ÷ trailing P/E) implies EPS of roughly **$10.50**, while trailing FCF (market cap × FCF yield) implies only about **$3.80/share** of free cash flow — a wide gap between reported earnings and owner cash.

For owner earnings, I weight toward the cash reality but allow that some of today's elevated capex is genuine growth investment (capacity for an AI/logic upgrade cycle) rather than pure maintenance spend, landing on a normalized owner-earnings estimate of roughly **$6.50/share** — blended between the $3.80 FCF figure and the $10.50 EPS figure. Assuming a 4-5% terminal growth rate (mature but still-growing WFE market, tempered for cyclicality) and a 10-11% discount rate (reflecting the 1.62 beta and real, if imperfect, moat), a normalized-earnings multiple of 15-20x — well below the market's current 32-51x — is the appropriate multiple for a capital-intensive, cyclical business with this quality of moat. That produces a fair-value range of roughly **$95-$135/share**.

Against an implied current price near $535, that's a margin of safety of roughly **-78%** — the stock is priced for a business that never has a down-cycle and converts far more of its earnings to cash than it currently does. This isn't a story of a bad business; it's a story of a good, cyclical business priced like a monopoly at the peak of a capex supercycle.

## The Cloning Caveat
Two superinvestors are in this name. John Armitage's Egerton Capital initiated a new position sized at 3.64% of portfolio — a meaningful, if not enormous, allocation from a concentrated global long/short manager, and worth taking seriously as corroboration. Chase Coleman's Tiger Global added 85% to an existing stake, but the resulting position is still only 1.14% of portfolio — a modest add, not a statement of high conviction. Neither is a 20-40%-of-portfolio bet that would force a much harder look regardless of valuation; both read as real but moderate-conviction interest, which is useful corroboration of the moat thesis but says nothing about whether today's price is sensible — and by this analysis, it isn't.

## Verdict
**Pass**, conviction 2/10. The business is understandable, the moat is real (7/10), and the ROE/leverage combination hints at capable management — but predictability is undermined by a large earnings-vs-cash-flow gap and a market pricing in an unusually steep forward-earnings jump, and the price implies roughly a -78% margin of safety against a conservative owner-earnings estimate. Munger's filter applies: wonderful business, not at this price.
momentum_thesis: AMAT's tape is a textbook late-cycle momentum name: +204.9% over 12 months, +77.8% over 6, +31.5% over 3, but the last month rolled over -8.4% and RSI14 has cooled from what was almost certainly overbought territory to a neutral 52 — this reads as a monster AI-capex-driven run now digesting, not a fresh breakout. Trading 41.6% above its 200DMA with a 1.62 beta, the stock is priced for perfection and any market-wide de-rating in semicap names lands with amplified force. Positioning offers no cushion on the way down: short interest is a token 2.11% of float with only 1.34 days to cover, so there's no squeeze fuel to buy against a drawdown, and the 1.21 put/call OI ratio reads more as longs quietly hedging gains after a 200% run than as smart money pressing a fresh bearish bet. Egerton's brand-new 3.64%-of-portfolio initiation in Q2 2026 and Tiger Global's 85% share add in Q1 2026 confirm real institutional conviction chasing the trend right into the highs — supportive of persistence, but it also means the crowd buying is exposed to the same air pocket with nothing underneath to absorb it. Net: this is a trend to respect, not chase at current levels — the setup favors adding on a pullback toward the 200DMA over paying up here.
